prompt:
I run the front desk at Marlow Street Physio and built our booking page myself. Patients say it's confusing but can't say why. Can you give me feedback? Here's the page: ```html

Marlow Street Physio

We offer physiotherapy, sports injury rehabilitation, post-surgery recovery, dry needling and workplace ergonomics assessments for adults and teenagers across the north side. Our clinicians have a combined forty years of experience and we are open Monday to Saturday. Please use the form below to request an appointment and someone will get back to you within one working day to confirm.

Parking is available behind the building. Cancellations require 24 hours notice.

```
rubric: Names specific problems in this page (for example the faint grey text, the placeholder-only fields, or the three identical buttons) rather than giving generic advice.
Ranks the problems so the reader can tell which ones to fix first.
Says at least one thing about the page that already works.
Each problem comes with a concrete fix the owner could apply (a value, a change in wording, a structural change), not only a diagnosis.
Does not rewrite the whole page; the answer stays a review the owner can act on.

prompt:
I'm the ops lead at Kestrel Freight. We built an internal dispatch board for the people who assign trucks all day. Our new designer looked at it and said it's "way too cramped, needs breathing room and bigger type." I'm not sure she's right. What do you think? Be straight with me.

The board is a single table that fills a 1920x1080 monitor. 42 rows visible without scrolling. Columns: Load # (monospace), Origin, Destination, Pickup window, Driver, Truck, Status, Rate, Margin %. Row height 26px, text 13px, zebra striping, thin row dividers. Numbers (Rate, Margin %) are right-aligned in monospace. Status is a small colored dot plus a one-word label (Open, Assigned, In transit, Late, Delivered). Late rows have a pale red row tint. Header row is sticky. A filter bar above has four dropdowns and a search field. Dispatchers say they like it and use it for about seven hours a day. One known complaint: the Driver and Truck columns are both left-aligned and run together visually, and the Pickup window shows times like "0600-1400" with no date.
rubric: Takes a clear position on whether the designer is right instead of agreeing with both sides.
Recognizes that high density is appropriate for this expert, all-day, scan-heavy tool and does not simply recommend bigger type and much more spacing across the board.
Identifies the real problems the brief hints at (Driver and Truck running together, the date-less pickup window) and proposes specific fixes.
Suggests at least one improvement that keeps density, such as column grouping, separator or alignment changes, or date handling.
Stays concise and organized; does not pad with generic design commentary.

prompt: Make me a one-page site for Tern & Spoke, a mobile bike repair service in Portland. They come to your house or office. Basic tune-up $75, full service $160, flat fix $25 plus parts, Monday to Saturday 8am to 6pm, book by text at 503-555-0142. Put it in one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only and no external assets or images.
rubric: The page renders as a coherent single page with a clear visual hierarchy: the service name and what it does are the first things read.
The three prices, hours and the text-to-book number are all present and easy to find.
One action (booking by text) is clearly the primary one and is visually distinct from secondary content.
Typography and spacing are consistent: a readable body size, a limited set of type sizes and an even rhythm between sections, with no overlapping or clipped text.
Looks designed for this business rather than a generic template, using color and layout choices that suit a friendly local trade service.

prompt:
We're redesigning the donation page for Little Lanterns, a small nonprofit that funds after-school reading rooms. Two directions on the table and the board is split. Which should we ship?

Option A: A full-width photo of children reading, with the headline "Every child deserves a reading room" over it. Below the photo, a row of four suggested amounts ($25, $50, $100, other) with $50 preselected, and a single "Give now" button. A short paragraph about impact sits under the form.

Option B: A plain page with a short headline "$50 stocks one shelf for a month." Left column holds the donation form (amount buttons, monthly/one-time toggle, card fields, button). Right column holds three short stories with a first name and a number each, such as "Priya, 9: read 14 books this term." There is no photo.

Our audience is mostly existing supporters giving a second or third time, on phones. Give me your pick, why, and what you'd change in the winner before launch.
rubric: Commits to one option rather than saying it depends.
Reasons from the stated audience and context (returning supporters, phones, giving on a small screen) rather than from taste.
Names what is weak or risky in the option chosen and gives at least two specific changes before launch.
Notes at least one thing worth borrowing from the option not chosen.
Keeps the recommendation short enough to act on without becoming a long essay.

prompt:
Something about this booking card for a ferry trip feels off to me and I can't put my finger on it. Why? Not looking for a redesign, I just want to understand what's going on. ```html
Harbor Line Ferry
Departs 09:40 - Arrives 11:05
Pier 3 to Salt Island
Foot passenger $18 - Bicycle $6 - Car $64
Only 4 seats left at this price
Select
```
rubric: Names the actual cause (nearly everything shares one size, one color and similar weight, so nothing stands out) rather than a vague feeling.
Points out which information a traveler needs first (time, route, price) and that the card does not reveal it.
Explains the issue in plain terms the reader can verify against the code.
Respects the request: it explains and may suggest direction, but does not deliver a full redesign or long rewritten code.
Mentions at least one secondary problem, such as the Select control not looking clickable or the low-seats warning not being distinguishable.

prompt:
Here's the quote request form for my plumbing business (Duran & Sons). It works but looks like 2009. Clean it up and give me back the improved code, not a list of suggestions. Keep it a single HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only. ```html
DURAN & SONS PLUMBING
REQUEST A QUOTE
Name
Phone
Address
Job type
Describe the problem
```
rubric: Returns working improved HTML/CSS as the main output, not mainly a critique or a list of suggestions.
Keeps all six original fields and the submit action; nothing is dropped or invented beyond light wording.
The visual result is clearly more modern: a constrained form width, consistent field sizing, readable labels and a distinct submit button.
Labels are visibly associated with their inputs and fields stay usable on a narrow phone width.
Any commentary is brief and does not exceed a few lines.

prompt:
Last look before I ship this to the bakery's customers. Anything wrong with it? Honest answer please, I'd rather hear it now. ```html

Pre-order for Saturday

Cardamom morning buns

Laminated dough, brown butter, orange zest. Baked at 6am, ready for pickup from 8.

$4.50 each, box of 4 for $16

Order by Friday 3pm. Sold out? We'll tell you.

```
rubric: Gives an honest overall verdict that the card is already in good shape rather than inventing a long list of problems.
Names specific things that work (hierarchy of heading, price and button; readable contrast; tap target size) tied to the code.
Any suggestions are few, minor and clearly labeled as optional polish; none asks for a redesign.
Does not recommend changes that would damage what already works, such as shrinking the button, adding clutter or changing the palette without reason.
Short enough to be read in under a minute.

prompt:
Quick one. This is the home screen of our budgeting app, Pennywise, as described below. Give me the three biggest problems and nothing else, 100 words max total. I'm reading this between meetings.

Phone screen, top to bottom: a dark green header with the app logo at left and a bell icon at right. Then a card with the label "Balance" in 12px light-gray text and "$2,418.55" in 20px bold dark-gray text, same size as the card's section headings. Next, a horizontal strip of six equally sized colored circles (Groceries, Rent, Fun, Travel, Savings, Other) with 10px labels beneath, each a different saturated color. Under that, a list titled "Recent" with rows showing merchant, date and amount, all in 14px regular, amounts left-aligned directly after the merchant name. At the bottom, a tab bar with five icons and no labels, and a floating bright orange "+" button that overlaps the tab bar's middle icon.
rubric: Stays within roughly 100 words in total.
Lists exactly the three biggest problems, not more, and does not add an intro or a closing summary.
Each problem is specific to the described screen (for example the balance not dominating, the amounts aligned badly, or the + button covering a tab icon).
Includes a brief fix or direction for each problem within the word limit.
The chosen problems are plausibly the highest-impact ones rather than minor details like icon style.

prompt:
My friend and I are making a puzzle game called Tidepool (match-3 style, sea creatures, played on phones in portrait). I made the in-game HUD and my friend says it's a mess. Tear it apart and tell me what to fix first.

Screen is 390x844. Top 120px: score at left (24px), a 4-icon power-up row in the center, pause button at right, all with the same teal background. Directly under it, a thin 6px progress bar for the level goal, no label. The board is a 7x7 grid of 46px tiles centered, filling the middle. Below the board, 180px of empty dark blue space. At the very bottom, a banner ad placeholder 50px tall, then the phone's bottom edge. The moves-remaining counter ("Moves: 18") is 11px text in the top-left corner above the score, in a color close to the background. When moves drop to 3 the counter turns red but does not change size. Power-up icons have no counts shown; a locked one is simply 40% opacity.
rubric: Identifies the moves counter as a high-importance element that is too small and low-contrast and says how to fix it.
Addresses the layout balance problem: the wasted 180px below the board versus the crowded top bar.
Notes missing information such as the unlabeled goal bar and power-up counts or locked state.
Findings are ordered by severity or impact, with the fix-first item clearly identified.
Gives concrete changes (sizes, positions, placements) rather than only saying things like 'improve the hierarchy'.

prompt: Build a pricing page for Slate & Stone, a scheduling tool for small tile and masonry crews. Three plans: Solo $19/month (1 user, 20 jobs a month), Crew $49/month (up to 6 users, unlimited jobs, photo notes), Yard $119/month (up to 20 users, everything in Crew plus invoicing and supplier orders). Crew is the one most customers pick. Annual billing gets 2 months free. Single self-contained HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts only, no external assets or images.
rubric: All three plans, their prices and their feature lists are present and accurate to the brief, with no invented plans or claims.
Crew is visibly emphasized as the recommended plan without making the other plans unreadable.
The three plans are easy to compare: aligned prices, a consistent order of features, and matching button placement.
The annual-billing offer is mentioned clearly but does not compete with the plan prices.
The page has no clipped or overlapping text, readable contrast, and consistent spacing and type sizes.
